entry.title: Math.random() Is Not a Secret: Session Key Lessons From the Check Point Intrusion Campaign
entry.summary: The attacker did not guess the admin password. They predicted the random number generator. That is the first step in an intrusion campaign described this week by GreyNoise, a threat intelligence company. The attacker started a few logins on a small file server, collected the "random" values it sent back, and worked out the server's secret cookie key from them. With that key they made their own admin cookie and took over the server. They then used that server as a relay to control and steal data from 24 Check Point Security Management Servers at 22 organizations. Below: the two weak points in that chain, why Math.random() can be predicted, and fixes in Node.js, Java and Python, plus checklists for Check Point and HFS admins. A note on sources: everything below comes from the GreyNoise repor…

entry.title: StorePulse, a free read-only health check for nopCommerce
entry.summary: Most nopCommerce problems don't crash the store. They fail quietly: The scheduled task that sends emails stops, and order confirmations sit in the queue for days. The same error is logged thousands of times a day, and nobody opens the log. Bots create guest customer records until the database is several gigabytes bigger than it should be. A plugin fails to load after an update, and the feature it provided just disappears. nopCommerce already keeps the data that shows all of this. It's spread across the log, the message queue, the scheduled tasks and the settings, so you only see it if you know where to look. We built StorePulse to look in all those places at once. entry.title: 三丰云免费云服务器实测：一次误删后的环境重装，顺手把备份脚本补对了（半年运维记录）
entry.summary: 先纠正一处说法：上一版我说“自动备份跑得很稳”，其实是错觉——脚本确实在跑，但备份文件从没验证过能不能还原，直到上个月一次误操作才补上了这一课。 事情很平常。我在整理站点目录，想清掉旧 Typecho 主题的残留文件，路径写错了一级，rm -rf 下去，连带 uploads 删掉一片。Nginx 还在转，页面图全白。第一反应是找备份：脚本每天凌晨三点打包，tar.gz 确实有，但我从没测过解包。 打开一看，有两个问题：一是脚本只打包了 /www/wwwroot/blog，没带数据库；二是压缩包写在本机同一块盘，磁盘写满时会静默失败，日志里只有空行，没有报错。也就是说，那份“备份”只能救一半。 补救分三步：先从旧压缩包里恢复 uploads 目录，图片还在；再用 mysqldump 把现有库导出一份；最后把脚本重写成“打包 + 导库 + 往另一台机器传一份”。前后大概两小时，站点停了一个半小时。 顺手把环境重来了一遍。系统是 Ubuntu 22.04，Nginx + PHP 8.1 + MariaDB，Typecho 放在 /www/wwwroot/blog。装完逐项对了一遍：PHP 扩展、伪静态、证书、时区、swap。意外发现 swap 之前一直没开，1G 内存跑 MariaDB 偶尔 OOM；补了 1G swap 后就再没出现过。 资源这边，装完是这个样子：负载常年 0.2~0.5，内存占用不到一半（MariaDB 加 PHP-FPM 大概 400MB 出头），磁盘每周涨几百 MB，主要是备份目录和日志。这个量级说明它就是个轻量练手环境，别往上叠重活。 续期还是老规矩：7 天一次，进控制台手动点，有效期立刻刷新，IP 和数据都不动。我设了每周一的手机提醒，半年下来没漏过一次。它不是自动兜底的，得你自己花 30 秒。 我一开始用的是免费虚拟主机：通过 FTP 上传、在面板里建库、改 PHP 版本，够跑静态站和一个小博客。虚拟主机偶尔有维护公告，面板会提前挂出来，重启那段时间站点会短暂 502。后来要装 Nginx、要写自己的脚本，才换成免费云服务器。两条路都能走，看你要不要 root。 手动续期：7 天一次，成本就是点一下 配置透明：1核1G、5M 带宽，控制台写的和实际跑的对得上 数据没丢：三十来次续期，配置和库都在 快照恢复：折腾崩了能从系统盘快照拉回来 工单能处理：提过一次 VNC 黑屏，等了大概四个小时，最后换浏览器内核解决 文档够看：Nginx、PHP、数据库的常见问题有中文条目 环境不挑：apt 装什么是什么，没有奇怪的源 监控够用：面板负载曲线跟实际对得上 不承诺永久：也不承诺 SLA，写明了是实验性质 适合当备份机：我拿它跑第二份备份，多一份心里踏实 学生课设、Linux 命令练习、Typecho 或 WordPress 博客、小 API 调试、定时脚本、给笔记做第二份备份。不适合对外正式业务，不适合高并发，也不适合当唯一数据源；它是轻量实验环境，不是生产级高可用方案。 想试的自己搜官网，注册后实名、创建实例。第一件事别急着装博客，先把备份脚本写对，然后手动还原一次，看看能不能真的跑起来。新手可以先从免费虚拟主机熟悉操作，再迁到免费云服务器。

entry.title: A Memory Exhaustion Bug in Logbook, and Six Review Comments That Made My Fix Better
entry.summary: This post is about a fix I am working on in Zalando Logbook, and about a code review that taught me more than the fix did. Logbook's servlet integration logs HTTP requests and responses. To log a body, it first copies the whole thing into memory. That is fine for normal traffic, but issue #2441 points out the risk: a very large or never-ending body means the server keeps buffering until it runs out of memory. That is a denial-of-service problem. Someone does not need to break in to take a service down, they only need to send a huge request. My PR (#2442) adds a size limit, maxBufferSize: Once a body goes over the limit, Logbook stops keeping a copy and drops what it had stored. entry.title: Where Did the Year Go? Blame Your Brain's Compression
entry.summary:
It's late November. Think back to March. What do you actually remember? Probably a launch, a trip, one odd conversation. The rest has folded into a blur. Nine months, and most of them don't have a name. Now think of a summer when you were ten. It felt endless. A single week had a beginning, a middle and a story. The clock was the same. What changed is what your memory kept. Memory seems to work a little like compression. Ordinary days that look alike get folded into one. A new place, a first attempt or a surprise gets stored on its own, so it takes up more room when you look back. Two ideas are usually offered for why time speeds up with age, and researchers haven't settled on one answer: Proportion: a year is a tenth of a ten-year-old's life, but a fortieth of a forty-year-old's. Novelty: childhood is full of firsts, and adult weeks mostly aren't. You can check the second one yourself. Try to describe last Tuesday. Then last Wednesday. If you can't tell them apart, they've already been compressed. Two weeks of stand-ups, tickets and pull requests, and when the retro arrives you can barely say what happened. But the week you shipped something strange, or finally learned a tool you'd avoided, you remember in detail. Busy is not the same as memorable. You don't need a trip to Japan. You need small breaks from your routine that give your memory something new to store: Take a different route to work, or to the shop. Learn something unrelated to your job, for example a language, an instrument or a recipe. Build one small, pointless thing just because it's fun. Talk to someone outside your usual circle. Once a week, write one line: what was new this week?
That last one is the changelog. In a month you'll have a record of days that weren't identical, and writing it also makes you look for something worth writing. We aren't running out of time. We're running out of moments that feel different from the ones before them. So here's my question: what's the last new thing you did that made a week feel longer?
